drills.q: Name the three required elements of a disciplined chaos experiment and what specifically goes wrong if each is skipped.
drills.a: A falsifiable, specific hypothesis (skip it: no way to tell if you learned anything). A bounded blast radius (skip it: the experiment can become an actual uncontrolled outage). A pre-defined, measurable abort condition with a real person watching (skip it: nobody has the authority or trigger to stop things before they cascade).

drills.q: Explain what Toxiproxy does mechanically and why fault injection through it doesn't require touching application code.
drills.a: Toxiproxy is a TCP proxy placed between the service and a real dependency; the service connects to the proxy instead of the dependency directly, and faults ('toxics': latency, bandwidth limits, timeouts, connection resets) are toggled on/off externally via Toxiproxy's HTTP API. Because injection happens at the network/proxy layer rather than inside the application, no test-mode branches are needed in the code, which keeps the experiment realistic (it exercises the real production code path) and trivially reversible.

drills.q: A team's pod-kill chaos experiments (via Litmus/Chaos Mesh) pass cleanly every time, but the service still fails badly when a real downstream dependency becomes fully unreachable. Diagnose.
drills.a: Pod-kill chaos tests the orchestration/infrastructure layer -- whether Kubernetes correctly detects and replaces a killed pod -- which is a different failure layer from application-level handling of a slow or unreachable dependency connection (retries, circuit breakers, fallback logic). Passing pod-kill tests says nothing about that second layer; the team needs network/connection-layer fault injection (Toxiproxy-style latency, timeout, or blackhole faults) specifically to exercise and validate the application's own resilience code.

drills.q: Why did Netflix build Chaos Monkey, and what specific organizational pain was it addressing?
drills.a: After Netflix moved to AWS, instance failure became a frequent, expected event rather than a rare one, and engineers needed services that were genuinely fault-tolerant, not just services whose fallback code looked correct in review but had never actually been exercised (and could have silently bit-rotted). Chaos Monkey randomly terminated production instances during business hours specifically to force continuous, real validation of fault tolerance, with engineers present to observe and respond immediately rather than discovering gaps from unattended logs later.

drills.q: Walk through the full structure of a game day from planning through retrospective, naming the step most commonly skipped and why that skip matters.
drills.a: Pick one specific, plausible failure scenario; write and get sign-off on a falsifiable hypothesis and measurable abort condition beforehand; assign explicit roles (fault injector, dashboard watcher monitoring the abort condition, note-taker, incident commander with real abort authority); run the injection against a bounded scope; hold a retrospective. The most commonly skipped step is converting retrospective findings into a tracked, owned fix with a deadline -- without it, a discovered resilience gap just quietly persists until the next game day (or production) rediscovers it.

drills.q: Why do the Principles of Chaos Engineering call for running experiments in production or production-like environments, rather than staging, and what makes this safe?
drills.a: Staging environments systematically fail to reproduce real production's actual traffic patterns, data shapes, and scale, so a staging-only chaos program risks validating the wrong thing entirely -- confidence that doesn't transfer to real conditions. Safety in production comes from the discipline itself (bounded blast radius, a pre-tested abort mechanism, mature observability to detect the abort condition quickly), not from avoiding production altogether.

drills.q: A staff engineer proposes moving from quarterly human-run game days to continuous, automated chaos experiments in production, Netflix-style. What has to be true first, and what's the honest risk of skipping the prerequisites?
drills.a: Continuous automated chaos requires the hypothesis/blast-radius/abort-condition discipline to work without a human curating each run: automated, reliable steady-state measurement; an automated, tested abort/rollback mechanism that doesn't depend on a human noticing in time; and observability mature enough to attribute a specific degradation to the specific injected fault rather than unrelated noise. Skipping these while only automating the scheduling of fault injection reproduces the 'experiment becomes a real incident' failure mode, just on an unattended, higher-frequency, harder-to-catch cadence -- automating the cadence is the easy part; automating trustworthy detection and abort is the harder prerequisite most orgs underestimate.

drills.q: Your team's chaos game days have confirmed the same hypotheses cleanly every quarter with no surprises. Should the program be scaled back, and how do you decide?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- repeatedly confirming a hypothesis is genuine evidence a resilience property still holds as dependencies, code, and traffic patterns evolve, so 'still true' is real, non-wasted information. Scaling back is warranted only if the hypotheses themselves have stopped being meaningfully risky or informative; the correct response then is escalating blast radius or targeting newer, previously-untested failure modes (a recently added dependency, a recently changed critical path) rather than stopping the program, prioritized by tracking which parts of the dependency graph haven't yet been exercised.

drills.q: How do you decide the appropriate blast radius when running an entirely new type of chaos experiment for the first time, and what does it mean if even the smallest reasonable scope feels too risky to run?
drills.a: Start at the smallest scope that can still produce a meaningful signal -- one instance, one canary, single-digit percent of traffic -- and only escalate after that smaller step runs cleanly (hypothesis confirmed, abort condition never triggered) at least once; never start a new, untested experiment type at wide blast radius regardless of confidence. If even the smallest version feels too risky to run at all, that itself is useful information: the system likely isn't ready for chaos testing of that specific failure mode yet, and the actual next step is improving observability/rollback capability first, not skipping the experiment and hoping it would have gone fine.

drills.q: A circuit-breaker fallback path passed code review but failed the first time it was actually triggered in production. What's the root cause pattern, and what chaos-engineering practice prevents recurrence?
drills.a: Root cause: the fallback path was never empirically exercised since it was written, so it silently bit-rotted -- a config value drifted, a downstream API shape changed, or a latent bug went unnoticed because the path never actually ran. Prevention: run the specific fault that triggers this path (via Toxiproxy or equivalent) as a recurring, automated CI or scheduled check rather than a one-time manual verification, so the fallback is continuously proven to still work as the surrounding system changes.
